title: The Solar System sorted its planet-building ingredients from the very beginning
topic: Solar System & Planetary Science / Planet Formation
freshness: Published September 18, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: Meteorite chemistry suggests that, within the Solar System’s first million years, the material building the earliest small worlds was already being sorted. Those first bodies contained unusually large amounts of heat-processed rocky beads and much less fine, ice-rich dust than later bodies.
whyItMatters: Planet formation was not simply a matter of nearby material clumping together. The young Solar System was separating different ingredients almost from the start, which changes how scientists reconstruct the raw materials that eventually became planets, moons and asteroids.

body:
## The first rocks were already a sorted sample

Meteorites are the leftovers of the first small bodies, the planetesimals, broken up and delivered to Earth. Their chemistry, in a Nature Astronomy paper published on 18 September 2026, says the sorting started within the Solar System’s first million years. The earliest of those bodies were already enriched in heat-processed rocky beads and depleted in the fine, ice-rich dust that shows up more strongly in bodies that formed later.

The beads are chondrules: millimeter-scale droplets of melted rock, cooled quickly, later glued into larger stones. “Heat-processed” in the notebook’s summary means that melting happened before the planetesimal assembled. The fine dust is the other ingredient, colder, often carrying ice and the unmelted grains. A body built from an excess of chondrules and a deficit of that dust did not form from a random scoop of the disk. Something had already separated the ingredients.

The paper’s title is the mechanism the authors favor: aerodynamic sorting. In a gas disk, solids of different sizes feel drag differently. Small dust stays coupled to the gas. Larger beads drift, concentrate, and can be gathered into clumps while the fines are left behind or arrive later. Yale’s account, republished by Phys.org, frames the same result as the early Solar System choosing heat-processed rock over ice for its first bodies. The frame is vivid. The measurement is the meteorite mix and its timing.

## Timing is the part that changes the story

“Within the first million years” is early even by disk standards. The gas disk around the young Sun lasts a few million years, not a few hundred million. If the first planetesimals are already a sorted, chondrule-rich population at the one-million-year mark, then planet formation did not begin with a well-mixed sludge that only later differentiated. The separation of materials is part of the birth of the small bodies, not a cleanup that happened after planets existed.

Later bodies, with more of the fine ice-rich dust, then sample a disk that had evolved, or a region the early sorting did not empty. The inner Solar System’s dry asteroids and the outer Solar System’s icy ones are the grown-up version of a contrast that, on this result, was already underway at the planetesimal stage. Do not let that rhyme become a proof. The paper is about the earliest small worlds’ compositions. It is not a new map of every asteroid class.

## What is measured, and what is the drag model

Measured, via meteorite chemistry: early planetesimals, unusually rich in once-molten rocky beads, poorer in fine icy dust than the bodies that formed after them, and a clock that puts this inside the first million years. Interpreted: aerodynamic sorting in the gas disk governed those compositions from the outset, which is the claim in the title and the claim a reader should pressure-test in the paper. Drag is a well-established disk process. Applying it as the governor of these particular meteorite groups is the authors’ step. Other ways to concentrate chondrules exist. The paper is arguing this one fits.

Phys.org is a secondary write-up of the Yale account, not a second dataset. Nature Astronomy (the article linked in the sources) is the authority for the chemical argument and the timing. The next mechanism to understand, if this one holds, is the drag law itself: which particle sizes move which way, and how a disk that is mostly gas ends up building the first rocks out of the beads it has already melted.
